utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd like to begin the proceedings with a brief oral application for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll begin in open session and then I'll request leave to go into private session for part of the application. This is an application for protective measures for Witness KRAJ 165. We requested that he be permitted to testify with a pseudonym and with facial distortion and in private session for those portions of his testimony which will reveal identifying information. I'd like to refer initially to the tests set up by Your Honours in your oral decisions on the 13th of April and repeated on the 27th of April, 2005. Your Honours said that in order to show a real risk that revealing the identity of a witness could result in danger to that witness, there must be some objective evidence. That objective evidence can be demonstrated through such circumstances as a combination of the following three factors: 1, the expected testimony of the witness may antagonise persons who continue to reside in the territory in which the crimes were committed, for example, by implicating those persons in crimes; 2, the prospective witness or his or her family live in that territory, have property in the territory, or have concrete plans to return to that territory; 3, a general security situation which is unstable and is particularly unfavourable to witnesses and the families of witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. In respect of the third limb of that test, we rely on the UNHCR report of January 2005, which we've previously submitted to Your Honours, and Your Honours have stated that that report states that "the climate in Bosnia and Herzegovina remains unfavourable to persons who are resident there or have family resident there and who wish to fully discharge their duty to testify before the Tribunal." Now, I'd now request to go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber just has conveyed to the parties, after having heard arguments for the protective measures sought by the Prosecution, that it will give a decision as soon as possible, most likely today, even if not yet a full reasoned decision. Are you -- is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness? The three of you -- Ms. Edgerton is new, so I take it, Ms. Edgerton, that it will be you who's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova will be taking the next witness. Ms. Edgerton and I will be excusing ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I mention one matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Josse, welcome. I had not given up the hope yet to have a wig in court, but unfortunately you don't wear them in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was desperate to take mine off, so being able to represent the client without a wig is a real pleasure to me, I have to say. Your Honour, Mr. Stewart asked me to hand out copies of the document from the high representative that was mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've given one to Mr. Tieger and I have copies for Your Honours and the rest of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the decision in view of the last witness, of which Mr. Stewart would like to have the whole document presented. Yes. Mr. Registrar, could you already assign a number to it. It would be a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Defence Exhibit D44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Usher, could I ask you to escort the next witness. Do we have protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. He testifies without protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tokaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no translation? Is Mr. Tokaca on the right channel? You are now. Mr. Usher, could you please -- Mr. Tokaca, before giving evidence I would like to invite you to make the solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tokaca. You'll first be examined by Ms. Richterova, counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tokaca. Would you be so kind and state your full name and date and year of your birth.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: My name is Mirsad Tokaca. My father's name was Smajo. I was born on 28th July, 1954, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the Court's permission I would lead the witness through the educational and occupational background very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear no objections, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you obtained a diploma of the political science faculty in Sarajevo? You also studied --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: This is what I graduated from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's practical if Ms. Richterova puts to you all these data and whenever there's anything wrong, please interrupt her and correct her. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also studied the legal sciences and economics. You did the post-graduate work in the field of international relations, and you began your career as a journalist working for the TV Bosnia and Herzegovina. And later, you start working -- or you set up a company which dealt with financial management, marketing, and traffic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of time, have you achieved any other education or have you -- have you finished any theses apart from those I mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I have not completed any additional studies. However, after my post-graduate studies in international relations I am now involved in a thesis that deals with the role of the United Nations in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I hope that after the research that I have been involved in I will find the time to bring that work to an end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, you were involved in the work of the state commission for gathering facts on war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When was this state commission set up?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, I was the secretary of the state commission from August 1992. The commission was set up on the 28th of April, 1992, pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Already in May, June, and July I was invited to participate in the preparation of that work. And in August I was appointed the secretary of that commission and I stayed with this commission --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it possible that Mr. Usher would move little bit the ELMO because I cannot see the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what was the mandate of the state commission.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: It was to start gathering all the relevant facts and data, testimonies, documents, military orders, and instructions of the civilian authorities. And all those things that might be relevant for the court proceedings that we expected would take place and that would deal with the crimes committed during the war in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as of the beginning of war in April 1992. In addition to that, our task was also to set up relationships with the relevant international organisations that dealt with the same tasks, regardless of their affiliations, whether they were affiliated with the United Nations, a different state, or whether they were non-governmental organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, I would like to ask you to make your answers a little bit shorter because it's difficult to follow it and also for interpreters it's difficult to translate such long answers. You mentioned that your task was also set up cooperation but -- cooperation with other organisations. Apart from that, what other specific tasks did you have within the commission?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: We focussed on research; that was our main mission. We sought to find people who had information about war crimes. We talked to them. Based on their knowledge and interviews that we conducted with them, we wanted to obtain relevant data that would be forwarded to the judiciary organs in the future. That was the main part of our job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned interview. You interviewed people. Did you personally interview any witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes. We opted for interviews because it is a complex form and provide -- provides a lot of data. I conducted a series of interviews with the witnesses. I took their statements. I was in charge of the entire job. I was responsible for that. I had my associates who worked on the ground in Sarajevo and in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the condition of war were such that they imposed a need for me to work with the witnesses and to take statements from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many statements did you personally take and how many statements were taken by the commission as such?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I myself must have taken over a thousand statements. Every statement that was taken for the commission I read. Up to today, we have taken over 7.000 statements all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court the methodology of work you adopted. What -- after you take the statement or even before you take the statement, what -- what was the work you did?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: First of all it was very complicated to obtain statements and witnesses in the conditions that we faced. I worked in Sarajevo that was under siege all this time. We used all sorts of methods in order to cross over through the tunnel in order to find the witnesses and work with them. After we gathered documentation, that documentation would arrive in Sarajevo in our central office where the lawyers, historians, and sociologists analysed that documentation and that documentation would be classified according to the methodology that we set up, which was based on the four Geneva Conventions and two Additional Protocols, one being the protocol on genocide. Those documents were classified. We set up a code system and this was filed in our archives and before that the data was entered into our database.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go into your database, I would like to ask you -- you said you analysed, you store, and later you put -- you input data into your database. Until now, have you managed to enter all the data into your database?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Unfortunately we have not. The documents are numerous. We were -- faced a lot of problems during the war. Even after the war the work of the commission has been obstructed. That is why quite a lot of documentation has still not been analysed nor has been one -- part of the database. I don't know what the final destiny of the commission will be. Its status has still not been clarified. In the meantime, I and a group of associates have set up an association; that is a voluntary organisation. I'm a volunteer there. I did that in order to continue our work because the work of the commission from the Dayton Accords until today has been rather blocked and hampered with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the work was blocked and that you with other group of volunteers, you want to continue the work of the state commission. How long did you work for the state commission?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Until 2003.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: After that I became the president of the research and documentation centre. I would like to add that all the funds were interrupted in August 1998. That's why the commission was blocked in its work. I had to seek solutions in order to be able to continue this very important work, the research work that is very important, to my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that you continue working in this research and documentation centre. Is it a new type of work or do you continue what you started -- what you already started doing with the state commission?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Our main goal was continue the good tradition of the commission. In other words, we wanted to preserve our experiences, to build upon them, to continue collecting documents and statements, to continue the project of what we call oral history. And in addition to that, we wanted the activity of this documentation centre to be enlarged and to spread on to the gathering of other documentation that is filed in other institutions. We wanted to create a good quality archive and to also engage in the education of young people in the field. In other words, we wanted to set up one unique place where we would collect documents that could be relevant for providing answers to what happened during the period 1992 to 1995. So this research centre focuses on this period of time between 1992 and 1995 and everything that happened during that period of time, during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, do you work on any specific project within the research and documentation centrum?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: First we created a strategy which we called "facing the past." This strategy consists of several pillars or several very specific projects that we are involved in. One of the key projects that we started towards the end of 2003 is the project -- the working title is "the losses of population." I can go back to that project later on. In addition to that project, the losses of population, we also have another project called "oral history," also "the monitoring of case -- of legal proceedings." I believe that you know that the state court has started operating in Bosnia with a special focus on war crimes. We want to monitor the work of that institution. So the entire work of the research and documentation centre will have a number of aspects. In addition to that, we have established close cooperation with two similar documentation centres in Belgrade and in Zagreb. In Belgrade, this is the fund for humanitarian law and in Zagreb the centre for facing the past. We want to create the environment in the entire region which would serve as a forum for open discussion of all the war crimes. We want to create such an atmosphere in which potential witnesses who have never spoken to anybody come forward, talk about their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. experiences. We want to eliminate the cases of manipulation with a number of facts in our area. We want to talk through facts and through court decisions that have been handed down before this Tribunal but also before local courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, you describe now the -- in detail the purpose of the establishment of this centre. I would like to focus on this project called population losses. Did you set up also or created a database by working in the research and documentation centrum?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: That was a precondition for such a complex research. We set up a very modern and quality database in which we stored everything that resulted from our research. We wanted to find every individual victim and explain their destiny, irrespective of the fact whether they were civilians, whether they were soldiers, irrespective of their religious, ethnic, professional or social affiliation. This is what we were not interested in. We focussed on the victims. We wanted to find as much information as possible as to how that victim became victim in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if -- if I understand correctly, you are collecting information not only on crimes committed against Bosniaks, but also crimes committed against Serbs and Croats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I would like to ask Mr. Tokaca just briefly introduce his database showing the data he is storing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There has been a request by the witness could use a laptop computer. The Chamber has said that as long as it's perfectly clear what exactly he consults, that it would be no problem. If the witness introduces that database, how will this -- I don't take it that the witness will give his laptop to us at the end of his testimony of Court. How is this going to be tendered into evidence, the information that he gives?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In effect, I only wanted to explain to the Judges how -- how the research centrum works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind of data he is using. It's nothing else than to assist the Judges to understand the database. We don't seek to tender the database into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that some of the charts you'll present later are taken from that database?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then it's yes. And I take it that you're not going to explain it to us but that the witness is going to explain it to us. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As Your Honour knows, we've been forewarned of this and we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, if we press one of these buttons, which I don't know which we do -- computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what files can be found in your database.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Considering the amount of time that this would take up, I would just like to make it possible for you to appreciate the method we use when setting up the entire project. Here on the screen you can see a whole range of lists and figures with data and I'm going to show you about religious affiliation and then it refers to the ethnicity of the victims that we have seen in the course of this research. Then there is a reference once again to ethnic groups and municipalities. And we're talking about 112 municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the source of these documents used. Here you've got a whole range of different lists of institutions, individuals, et cetera. We're talking about 400 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, can you slow down --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I do apologise. So it is a whole range of different sources of information that we have been using because it is extremely important for us to try when it comes to each and every victim and dead person to explain the circumstances of their death. And in item 5, we have an indication of the way in which people were killed and then different types of documents, videos, written documents, questionnaires, newspaper articles, photos, tapes, and databases from different government and non-governmental institutions that we all use in order to be able to compare the data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I ask you to slow down, because you're developing a speed which is difficult for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] I do understand. So in the end we've got different types of documents that we are using here. In the end 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. You can see that there is a system of clarification of data on a legal basis. We've been using it, as I told you, in order to make sure that every single piece of information that we use, in statements, in different questionnaires, in databases, so that we can classify it all properly and that makes it easier for us to retrieve that information if we need it later on. I did mention that we use the system which is enshrined in the Geneva Convention and in other rules and regulations of international humanitarian law. And you can see we've got five categories -- that is to say six categories here and we're talking about protected individuals and so on and so forth. I don't want to be too long-winded, but I would just like to open the key part. [In English] It's too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You really have to slow down. It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm doing my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Ms. Richterova, perhaps you take a bit more lead --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm trying, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I wouldn't say that the methodology is not important, but this Chamber has been provided with the Milosevic testimony and it noted that approximately 80 per cent was the methods used and the quality of the work, but not much on what the work resulted in. So of course that's -- that's something that the Chamber is interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I understand and in fact I intended to make it a little bit shorter, but I will try now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do it the following way. I take it that you've familiarised yourself with it. Ms. Richterova will put questions to you. If you could give short answers and wait for the next question because it's difficult and you're not the only one who has problems with it. Please proceed, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, because we are focussing on people killed and missing and you also prepared the charts which we will be discussing in a short -- shortly, I only want you to explain to the Judges the way how you avoid duplications which always happen when creating a database and inputting information. If you could very briefly show the relevant file and explain in a few sentences how you avoid duplications.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: It was one of the extremely complex issues that we had to solve in the course of this research. Before I give you an answer, it is very, very important to give you the overall context and explain why we had to do that and both this Court and anyone else investigating war crimes will know that in an entire region there had been a great deal of manipulation with figures and very imprecise assessments of the number of victims. All that has been misused and abused in a number of ways, and so it was our intention throughout this project to arrive at an as accurate number as possible, but not just the number but the identity of victims. In the course of that process it used to happen that there was indeed a great deal of duplication when it came to the names of victims because the victims names came from a whole range of sources and sometimes there was duplication even coming from one and the same source. So it was one of the key tasks that we had to complete. Let me just quote one example so I can show you how we did it. For example, column 1 to the left where you see my arrow now, it refers to possible sources of data and here you have different indications and different sources of data that we used. Thereupon in column A you've got the X here. These are the victims in our database that we qualify "active" and they're the only ones that we consider because everything is either duplication or indications which are not supported by sufficient proof, data, that would make it sufficiently convincing from our point of view to think that it is a victim that has actually died. For example, Abaza Muhamed. I'm showing you the arrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, you said the word "active." If an entry is active, what criteria this entry has to fulfil?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: When we talk about so-called active entries means that we have more than 250.000 names in our database. In order to determine what data, what entries are considered active, as you can see out of three names, out of a total of three, we opt for a name which is supported by the most complete data. In this case, the example is Mr. Abaza Muhamed. Even though it is quite clear that there is his father here, Arif, and you've got the same name four times over and the same year of birth three times, 1949. So we've got a couple of repetitions of this name and family name in this database and we opted for this particular X because it provides us with the most complete set of data with reference to this same person. So by that token we've managed to eliminate from the database three names which represent duplications. In the same way we've tried to eliminate all the other similar cases from the database, that is to say having the repetition in different checks and forms because that would give us a different total. The X that you referred to is the key indication which means that in the sum total this is the final data. For example, we have 150.000 names in the database. These 90.000 that are marked by X are the so-called active entries and we consider them to be correct, or -- in other words we consider those to be the relevant data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this was sufficiently explained. And I would like you now to have a look at the charts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I don't know whether the witness was provided with the charts and the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the chart would be -- and let me just see what you called the chart, Ms. Richterova --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's the colour version of chart and drafts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one which goes through the municipalities and -- yes. And it goes from 3869 to 4053. Yes. That's clear. That would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that chart which is referred to of the killed and missing Bosnian civilians in 1992 will be prosecution exhibit 857.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, I see that there's no translation, Ms. Richterova --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We will provide the translation of the one of the charts, but it's very self-explanatory and we will ask the witness to explain exactly what the chart and the word means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to see if we can cut that short and save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just looking at the front page, it seems that it is about civilians in 1992, that is split up in 12 months. That on the chart we see at -- where it starts with one -- from one to two should then be January, from 2 until 3 should be February. This also explains why we go from 12 to 13 because that's the whole of the month --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of December. Then I see Ubijeni and Nestali, which seems to be -- Ubijeni the ones killed and Nestali the ones missing. We can get that from other sources. These are numbers that are totalled at the end. This is about Nestali. The second page would be about Bijeljina. And then one of the things that perhaps needed so more explanation is at the bottom it says "nacionalna struktura po popisu 1991." Is that the -- the 1991 census, how people reported their nationality. That would be on the first line Croats, on the second Bosniaks or Bosnians, on the third line Serbians, on the fourth line Yugoslavians, and then on the fifth line, "ostali" would be foreigners? Could I just check that with you, Witness, ostali.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, others. Then I see on the chart itself which is a bit of a pity that the -- the ones killed, if there are more who are missing then suddenly the line indicating those killed disappears, is hidden by the numbers of those missing. That's of course a consequence of using this pattern. We see it on the top -- we see still the numbers. But on the bottom the blue disappears behind the red. Yes. A little bit less of colour could have given us also a graphic insight. Does this explain more or less what such a page says? Yes. Ms. Richterova, please add whatever, but just looking at it not being a jury but professional Judges it might be more efficient to see what we already understand from what we see and then you add whatever we might not have understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour because I think these charts are self-explanatory. I have only a few questions. The first is:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You put titles "killed" and "missing." How did you set criteria who would be put into a category of killed and who would be put into a category of missing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: All persons whose identity has been established have been placed into the category of the killed. As to any persons that we are still searching for we don't know where certain body parts or entire bodies might be are still in the category of those who disappeared. So that was the basic key criterion as to why we've got these two categories here, killed, once the identity of the victim is known and has been established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "once the identity of the person was established." Do you need to input into your database a date of death in order the person would be put in the category of killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Precisely. The entire questionnaire includes a whole range of data with regard to each individual victim, name and surname, place of residence, the father's name, the date of death, the place of death, and an exact location as to where the body had been buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact when creating this chart, have you eliminated any data from your database?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, it was indispensable because for many people we still don't know the exact date of death. So we could only have this sort of table with reference to those people where we at least know the month and the year of their death so that you can have all these indications as indicated in these tables. In order to have that, you at least have to have the month and the year of death, otherwise we wouldn't have been able to compile these tables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you do not have this kind of information, what do you do with the data?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: We've dropped that data from these tables. Let me just tell the Court that this is not final data. This is simply indicative data as to a certain phenomenon, that is to say the phenomenon of killing people and having people disappear in a certain area and over a certain period of time. This is an ongoing process. I don't expect any major changes, but there will be changes in terms of figures. As you add new data into the database, the figures will change but this is just an indicative set of data with regard to the killing of people in a given area over a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go to the chart for the municipality of Foca. It is the fourth chart with the ERN 0422-3872. And you mentioned that in this chart is an error. Can you explain -- can you point which error occurred in this chart?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Certainly. Whilst preparing for this testimony I checked the database once again, and -- I mean it's an endless task basically, but it is particularly important for me to point this out. Number 33 in the first column -- I can't really say that it is a mistake because all those people had indeed been killed. However, if we did not know the exact date, the data will nevertheless have to be included in the system. And we are talking about 33 people who were indeed killed in 1992, but we don't have any more specific information about their killings. So that's why we entered the 1st of January, 1992, for all these people and that's why they've cropped up in this table and that's why I've asked you to drop those 33 people from that table. That's my first point. In column number 6 where the reference is to 201, 201 people killed. I came across one man whose family name read Masic in one place and somewhere else Mesic. And according to our system we found that it was a kind of duplication. However, those cases are extremely rare. So this is why I've warned you. Just to let you know that in as far as these tables are concerned we will make some minor changes, no major changes. But even as they currently stand they are quite reliable and they firmly confirm a certain phenomenon. Secondly, you've got numbers matched by names and family names, plus extra data. So these are not simply figures; these are figures behind which we've got names and surnames of individual people. And here in the case of Foca, for example, you can see what happened and over what period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on this chart, were you able to form any conclusion in relation to people killed and missing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to allow me to make another point before I answer this question. I think it's quite essential for the purposes of the Court. In 1996 for the UN committee led my Mr. Manfred Novak on the people who disappeared, I did a task for them, a project for them, on the basis similar graphs. And that's what gave me the idea to continue applying the same method and including people who were killed as well. Those graphs at the time were rather interesting and they almost fully overlapped with what I managed to draw up ten years later. I submitted that study to the Court and you may use it as you see fit. But basically, all the graphs that I submitted to you, starting with Nevesinja, Bijeljina, and so on and so forth basically indicate the appearance of a phenomenon in a very short period of time. It mostly happened within four months of 1992, people being killed, people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disappearing. You've noticed it probably, but maybe we should have used different types of graphs. But there is total overlap of people being killed, people disappearing. So all this tallies completely. And if we talk in terms of the time scale in Foca, for example, it all took place between April and August. So it is a very short period of time, basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also would like to ask you -- now we were -- a minute ago we were describing the difference between killed and missing. You also provided a list or chart in which you distinguished - and we can see it also in your database - you distinguished between civilians and soldiers. What are the criteria using and inputting this type of information? What is the source of information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, are you moving to another exhibit or --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we then perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We can do it now before the witness answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make that clear, yes. That would be a document without ERN numbers, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We are awaiting the ERN. I would like to use the one I think we provided you one version which has English unofficial translation attached to always relevant B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would love to say how many pages there are, put since it is all 1 out of 1 I would have to count them all. It's the IDC research documentation centre documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There are altogether 28 pages, 14 English, 14 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Prosecution Exhibit P858.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move to that, Ms. Richterova, would you allow me one or two questions to the witness. I saw that you highlighted in yellow on -- the months 4, 5, 6 in the year 1992. And then suddenly in Kalinovnik month 7 is included as far as killings are concerned. Has this a specific reason or is it just a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was just for me. I wanted to mark the things that I have spoken about. For example, in Nevesinje you can see that the yellow colour just remained as an internal marking. It has got nothing whatsoever to do with any relevant data. I just used this yellow marking temporarily and I didn't have the time to erase it. There are even some graphs where there's no yellow colour. In haste as I was preparing for this testimony, I just omitted removing this yellow colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- so it has no meaning. Then one other question. The top always indicates what municipality we're dealing with, and it also say Bosnaci. Does that mean that we are just -- that these -- these data only concern Bosnians in the sense of -- well, we have heard a lot of words, Bosniaks, very often put at the same level. But I take it that you'd rather not use that word Muslims. But at least Bosnian -- non-Serb Bosnians. Is that -- non-Serb, non-Croat, or is everyone included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm using the official name for the ethnic group called Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a constitutional category and I can't call people by any other name. There is another term in terminology which is not legitimate. Sometimes these people are referred to as Muslims or Bosnian Muslims. In this case they are ethnic Bosniaks. They are not Serbs, they are not Croats, they are not others, they are ethnic Bosniaks. As the Prosecutor said, we can produce such tables for any other ethnic group in Bosnia and Herzegovina which will depend on the needs of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just to be fully aware of what these data are about. Please proceed, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I have one more thing regarding this chart. It's a chart with ERN number 0422-3881. It says Doboj Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can Mr. Tokaca inform me --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that it was an error. What is the correct title of this chart?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, if I may take a moment of your time. Since the Honourable Judge asked me, I would like to say that there are two graphs here that I have submitted. In one of them there are Croats in Modrica and in Kotor Varos. This is the only exception to the whole group. This graph should be here. This is 04 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kotor Varos, and you see here Bosniaks --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The ERN number is 0422-4045. It is a little bit behind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see it's split up Kotor Varos -- not split up, but it gives two graphs and data, one for Bosniaks and one for Croats. Yes, that's good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go back to the other exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, P858.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can the witness be provided. It is only show and the witness can explain very briefly what kind of data or information can be -- can be obtained from his database. If we take the page number 1 which is entitled -- which title is "Total Number of Those Killed and Missing During the War Based of Cause of Death," we can see -- And I am referring to the municipality of Bratunac so that we are talking about the same -- same chart or list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can see that in this -- are you with me, Mr. Tokaca? We can see here that you put Bosniaks and Serbs. And again, we have "killed," "missing," "unknown," and "total number." This total number here which is 3.469, for what period -- which period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: All the data here covered the period between 1992 and 1995. This chart depicting the total number of killed and missing of 3.469 names for the municipality of Bratunac covers the period between 1992 and 1995. The first column refers to the killed people of Bosniak and Serb origin. In this table we do not go into the status of people during the war, whether they were civilians or soldiers. The fact is that they were killed. The next column covers the missing persons, and the following one covers the unknown circumstances of death. We also covered such situations in which we did not know at all what happened to the person. If you look at the next table, the table of the total number of killed segregated into the categories of whether they were soldiers or civilians, the data is somewhat different. However, the total is almost the same; it differs by one name. You have civilians in vertical columns, the ethnic structure is the same, and also you have soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Again, we do not know the status of nine Bosniaks and we do -- did not know for 28 Serbs whether they were civilians or soldiers. So the last column covers the status of these people during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to stop here because here I would like you to explain. How do you set criteria for date -- for calling someone civilian and calling someone a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: When you collect data and when you receive data on every individual victim, we receive those from various sources. We receive data from official sources, the ministry of defence, various institutions. Amongst that data we would come across the status of the person during the war. That was reliable information as to whether they were soldiers or civilians. Furthermore, we did not always trust the information that we had received. We sought additional information about the status of these individuals. For every person we wanted to be sure what their status was. We went as far as to visit the cemeteries, we took photographs of the places where they were buried. In many of those photographs, there are headstones depicting the names of the people. There is a number of sources of information based on which you can establish whether the person was killed as a civilian or as a soldier, in other words what their status was at the moment of their death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in case you cannot establish whether the person was civilian or soldier, what is your procedure?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: As you can see in the table, we then categorised them into the category status "unknown." We were sometimes not absolutely certain. According to some records, one person was a civilian and that same person was a soldier. When we could not decide what the truth was, we would put such a person under the category "status unknown," and status in this case refers to their status during the war at the moment of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I go back to the Exhibit P857 when we have this chart from various municipalities and you put title "civilians," did you -- did you exclude those status was unknown?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we can -- we don't need to go to any further details regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few questions on it. First, on the first page I see total number of those killed and missing during the war based on the cause of death. Well, first of all, I do not see any information about the cause of death. Is that correct? It says whether someone died or whether someone is missing or -- but it doesn't say anything about the cause of death. Is that a mistake or is that a translation problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is an exact translation and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could perhaps the witness please slowly read the top of the first page where it says -- I think it's -- forgive my pronunciation, [B/C/S spoken]. Could you read that line so that the interpreters could translate that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I read the Bosnian version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The table that covers the municipality of Bratunac. The total number of killed and missing according to the way they disappeared. This is the way they were disappeared. Either they were killed or they went missing. And there are numbers for Bosniaks, for the killed, for the missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to be a translation error, Ms. Richterova. That's one. The second question I would have is on the second one where it reads "Total Number of Those Killed and Missing During the War Based on Which Army They Belonged to." Now, I see that a lot of civilians, that's 2.037 civilians belonged to the Bosnian army and 105 civilians belonged to the Serbian army. That's at least what it says. Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid you're not right, Your Honour. Can you look at the two vertical columns. On the left-hand side let me just first tell you that the name of the table in Bosnian. "The Total Number of Killed and Missing According to the Status, the Civilian Or Military Status." The first column covers civilians. The number that you read out is civilians, Bosnian and Serbian civilians. The next column --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- that's perfectly clear. Then we have again a translation error here. Could you slowly read the title above this -- these data which starts with [B/C/S spoken]. Could you read that line just slowly so that the interpreters can translate it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Total Number of Killed and Missing." I believe that it would be better for me to "add according to their military affiliation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- yes, yes. It's just a translation error. It's perfectly clear that -- yes. And military affiliation as far as civilians are concerned is to what - how to say that - to what group they belonged, not saying that they were military but they are at the site of where the militaries were -- yes. Okay. That's clear. Could you please take care that we get the right translations --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I apologise and as I stated at the beginning it is really an unofficial translation prepared for the purposes of today's session because we didn't have time to obtain an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- one second. Yes. If we are talking about the municipality of Bratunac, are we talking about those who were killed in Bratunac or those who resided in Bratunac before -- and got killed or went missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case we are talking about those persons who resided in the municipality of Bratunac in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Yes, Judge Hanoteau has a question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not understood something; that's why I would like to ask you about the municipality of Bratunac. When you say "civilians, Bosniaks and Serbs," and you mention the figures, are these people who did not have anything to do with the army, with the military? Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were civilians and this is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now for the soldiers, the Bosniaks and the Serb soldiers mentioned here. Were these soldiers who resided in Bratunac or were they soldiers who were killed in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were soldiers who resided in Bratunac and who had their address, residence, in Bratunac in the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were they killed in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not all killed in Bratunac, probably. They could have been killed elsewhere. However, there are two criteria for our research and I could go into great length in subanalysing these graphs. In this case we were not interested in soldiers more or less. There is also the category of the location of death. However, the analysis that we have done so far for civilians, they all show the almost total overlapping of the place of death and the place of residence. In the case of soldiers, this will differ to a certain extent. Their place of residence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these persons that feature in these tables are persons who resided in Bratunac but there's nothing to say that they were killed in Bratunac. And the same is true of the civilians and of the soldiers. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're not right. These graphs that you are looking at are -- all refer to civilians. The graphs only cover civilians. Soldiers were never the subject of our analysis. We have not analysed where they were killed. This should be the subject of a special analysis for us to see about the soldiers -- 1.289 soldiers, to analyse where they were killed, whether they were killed in Bratunac or elsewhere. But this would be a special, a separate analysis if we wanted to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Canivell has a question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you provide us with the following information. Could you give us the figures for all the municipalities that are covered by the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't understand your question. The total number of victims in these charts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you indicate -- You've told us about Bratunac. Could you provide us with figures covering all the other places that are marked by the colour blue on -- in your map that is at the front of your documentation in the same way you have provided us with information for the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Maybe I can assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- to the witness. We have a map and so I would like Mr. Usher to show the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be some confusion. The map has not yet been presented to the witness. Are you going to deal with that anyhow, Ms. Richterova, the totals?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The Prosecutor is going to take care of that, so there's no need for you to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, I'm going to put questions to the witness on matters you've discussed already. It's not entirely clear how someone can be unknown in terms of his status of being missing or killed. I mean, how could there ever be -- either you have established, I do understand, on the basis of the remains of that person that he was killed. If he's not -- if his body has not been found or identified, is he missing or is he not missing? I mean, what's -- what could create the doubt there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no doubt when it comes to the killed or the missing. Are you confused by the table in which you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see. It's uncertain -- no, in that -- no, I'm mixing up two matters. Yes, I apologise for that. I find that you were able beyond doubt, because otherwise unknown -- you would say if there's doubt you would categorise them as "unknown." On numbers of as much as approximately 3.000, you are able to establish -- well, to such a certainty, to such a level of certainty on, well let's say, 99 and a half per cent whether they were civilians or soldiers. I'm asking this because, of course, in this Tribunal we know that it's very, very often not that easy to establish whether someone was a soldier, was a combatant, carried arms, even if not fully dressed in a uniform. So what surprises me is the percentage in which you could draw a clear conclusion and did not have to categorise that person as unknown as to his civilian or military status.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This percentage is indeed very small here. In Bratunac we were not sure only about the military status of 37 people. There are very well-organised records about the affiliation of people to certain military formations. This column covering soldiers can be analysed and broken down in all the military formations that were active in Bosnia and Herzegovina and we can provide all the details. For the purpose of this particular case, I have focussed on civilians. Whatever you can see here, you can be sure that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the percentage of the reliability on the status of civilians is very high. It is absolutely impossible that any of these people categorised as civilians were also soldiers. The only minor dilemma may remain with the soldiers. In our research we have come across situations in which we had information that a person was a civilian at the moment of death. And then subsequently their status was changed into a different category, the category of soldiers. Those are very rare situations. And to be honest, I have to tell you those are the situations when people wanted to benefit from their former status. In illegal way, they changed their status. However, we are talking about a small percentage of such people, but also it is up to the state organs to sort and deal with that. We used a number of sources, we obtained information on whether a person was a soldier, whether they wore uniform, whether they belonged to a certain military formation, or whether they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I come back to my first question because too easily I said that I was confused. And I might be confused again on a translation problem. May I take you to the first page where it said total number of those killed and missing during the war. And the wrong translation says "based on the cause of death," and we now understand that that should be their status as missing or killed. Now, on that first page we see that for the Serbians you have 616 killed and you have 13 missing. Ms. Richterova, you see in the translation that it's wrongly translated it says "civilians and soldiers." That's not what the original says. The original says "killed or missing." Now you have one "unknown." So I come back to my question. How do you establish whether it's unknown that someone -- you could not establish that he's killed, you could not establish that he's missing. What do I have to understand by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two interpretations for this number. There are two reasons. The first one is a mistake, and the second one is the fact that the people appeared outside the period of 1992 or 1995. I can check the name of that person and then I can provide you with more accurate explanation as to how come this person appears in this category as unknown. It is impossible for this person to appear in this category as unknown. It is absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it's a mistake we don't have to hear about it. If it's not a mistake and you don't come up with anything else, then we'd like to hear. If it is a mistake or if it is someone outside the period, then of course he should not be in the database, because the database is limited to, as you said, 1992-1995. Ms. Richterova, please proceed -- I'm looking at the clock as well. Could you give us an indication how much more time you would need if you would not be interrupted and disturbed by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be finished within 10 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, I have final questions to you. You have a map in front of you in -- yes, this one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could that be assigned an exhibit number, Ms. Richterova, if you would like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I don't intend to tender this map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's just to assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we need no number. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can see the municipalities which are covered in the indictment; however, you produced these charts for lesser municipalities. But are you still able to assist the Judges and tell them approximately the total number of people killed and that got missing during the year 1992 in these municipalities? And I don't expect that you will provide an exact number.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: You mean the ones that I did not include in these graphs or do you mean all those that you can see here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean all you can see there. And I'm asking this question based on your knowledge and based on your work for this research centrum. So you are dealing with these figures on a daily basis, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I deal with this on a daily basis, but I've prepared these graphs in a detailed manner, basically. They refer to one group and I've got the latest data here but only divided by municipalities and there are no references to the national ethnic make-up of victims. So if we take it from the east, for Bijeljina I've got the overall number at this present moment. We've got 1.237 [as interpreted] people who were either killed or disappeared and -- 127 [as interpreted] had been killed and 110 [as interpreted] disappeared. But at the moment I can't tell you what the ethnic make-up is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we take -- let's start with these 25 charts which you prepared for this trial. In these charts you focussed on killed and missing Bosniaks. Can you assist the Judges, and it is really a pure mathematics, how many Bosniaks were killed or got missing based on the findings? If we are referring to this chart -- to these charts.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: In these graphs we've got more than 10.000 names. So if we don't go any further than that, if we don't make any assumptions outside that overall number. So I'd just like to stick to the graphs I've got here and if you make a sum total it's about 10.000 and something. So for those 20-something municipalities. And that's what I can talk about at the present moment. Obviously the overall number is much greater than that, but I believe that the main point of my testimony is not to give you the exact figure, and I'm unable to do so at the present moment at any rate. But when it comes to these graphs here, I can state all that with a great degree of certainty. It's more than 10.000 names and it, I believe, paints a sufficiently clear picture of the events at that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you are saying 10 -- more than 10.000 names, we can understand that it is more than 10.000 of killed and missing people in 25 municipalities in the year 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, more than 10.000 killed or those who disappeared, civilians, Bosnians, between -- in that period in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the dates once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the dates because the interpreter didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: More than 10.000 people of Bosniak nationality in the period between April and the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Josse, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps I have one question before I give you an opportunity to do so. Witness, I'd like to ask you the following: If we look at the Bratunac figures you've given to us then it appears that in 1995 that we certainly have a high number of civilians compared to the other years and compared to the -- compared to the -- especially Bosnians. Could you give us an explanation for this almost 1.600 that are reported in 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I don't seem to have that particular graph or table in front of me. I'm not very sure what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see in what is now Exhibit P858, which is Bratunac in the various ways it is split up, where you have a table which is called "Total Number of Those Missing and Killed Based on Year of the Event," then you have broken it down. 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, and 1995 gives a relatively high number. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour, I was looking at the wrong table. I've got the one you mean in front of me. So this is the overall number of those killed and who disappeared according to each individual year from 1992 through to 1995. For the year 1995 you've got 1.572 civilians killed, seven soldiers, and 291 where we don't know their status. My explanation is that those were probably civilians who fled from Bratunac in the direction of Srebrenica in the period of time between -- or after 1992 and who found themselves there at the time of the Srebrenica events in 1995. So those were the people who found themselves in that particular geographical area. Once we start carrying out a detailed analysis -- You were quite right in asking this question as where these people had actually been killed. We will be able to establish that correlation between the place where people found themselves in 1992 and the place where they must have been killed. Many of them could have been killed in Bratunac itself in 1992, but in the same way, many could have been killed in other places including Srebrenica because the biggest wave of refugees went in the direction of Srebrenica. So that would be a separate table, but it doesn't actually change their status as to where they were living in 1992. And it was in this respect that we actually did two different things, two different approaches, first of all their place of residence in 1992 and afterwards what were the locations at which people could have been killed afterwards. So this is a very specific analysis that we're going to take a special interest in in the future, but we would basically want to see what happened to those people: where they went, and at what locations they were actually killed, because many of those were not just refugees. For example there were situations in which people were apprehended at one place and they were taken somewhere else and they were executed somewhere else altogether, which is not a part of that region. So my explanation for this in as far as Bratunac is concerned most of those people 1.572, I'm not talking all of them, most of them were actually executed during the events at Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This illustrates that the tables might not give the final answer. It's not of direct relevance, since Srebrenica 1995 is both territorially and in time beyond the scope of this -- of the case against Mr. Krajisnik. But at the same time it's perhaps illustrative for what the tables can tell us and what they cannot tell us. Mr. Josse. Cross-examined by Mr. Josse:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, your commission was set up on the 28th -- can you hear me now. Your commission was set up on the 28th of April, 1992. What was it called on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: State commission for the gathering of data on war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why on the 28th of April, 1992, was it given the title "war crimes"?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Presumably, because the war started in the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what information had got back to you about what was happening at that particular time? You personally, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Look, don't ask me questions about the decisions made by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I did a professional job. If you ask me for my personal history, I spent the war in Sarajevo, and since August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, no one asks you about decisions taken by the government. The question was: "And what information had got back to you about what was happening at that particular time?" So Mr. Josse wants to know what you learned about the events that were going on at that time. He doesn't ask you to clarify a decision taken by others. Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just clarify that question. What I need to know is whether you want me to tell you what was my personal knowledge between April and August or as of the time when I was taken on as the secretary of that commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you become the secretary of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: In August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. All right. Well, I -- that's my misunderstanding. I assumed you were involved from the start and I'll move on. In fact, I was going to ask you where you spent 1992, but I think you begun to tell us. I don't need to know exactly. You were in Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Well, I was quite specific in my answer. I spent the entire war in Sarajevo and the siege of Sarajevo as well. Officially I was appointed in August. However, as early as May I was invited to do some voluntary work in my professional capacity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, please listen to the questions carefully, answer them. You give additional information. If Mr. Josse might like to hear that information, then he'll ask for it. If he would like to hear other information, you'll listen to his next question and provide him with the information that he's seeking. So the question was whether it was right that you were in Sarajevo in 1992 and you affirmed that you were. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the time you were employed by the commission, who paid you? Which organisation paid you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: We were allocated funds from the state budget.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which state are we talking about, please, for the avoidance of any doubt?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: We're talking about the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the war ended, you continued to be employed by the same entity. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they employed you until relatively recently, from what you told us.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Even today officially and professionally I'm a civil servant and work at this international documentation centre is voluntary work I do so it's nothing to do with the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you are concerned, you undertake your work in an impartial manner. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have allegations of ethnic bias ever been made against you or your organisation? There are two questions there, really. Let's deal with your organisation first of all.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such allegations. It may have happened. I can't rule it out. But officially, on the part of any institution or anything like that, I've never heard any comments as to any ethnical bias on my part because everything we did we did with the intention to provide answers to problems of crimes against victims, no matter who those victims were in terms of their ethnic group. Of course you will understand that considering the circumstances it was very difficult for us to do the job no matter who the victim was. Sometimes it was outright impossible. But you can see it on the basis of the names of victims. We have actually recorded victims of all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tokaca, at no meeting or in the course of your giving evidence or at any stage in your professional life doing this job has anyone ever accused you of ethnic bias. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I've never been accused of that by anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that your commission have taken statements from 7.000 victims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us the ethnic breakdown, please, of those 7.000 statements.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I really don't have that information. I can't give it to you. But certainly there are people of different ethnic affiliations. A couple of days ago I had a meeting with somebody -- I'm basically interested in victims, you know, I'm not in the business of determining their ethnic affiliation. I talk to anyone who wants to talk to me or to people I find in the field. So I've never been interested in the ethnic affiliation of any victims, so it really doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it may be my fault, Mr. Tokaca, but would you agree that in the context of your work and your evidence to this Chamber, the ethnic breakdown of the 7.000 people your organisation has spoken to is of importance?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I really don't think that it is of any consequence in this respect because I prepared to come here and in relation to Mr. Krajisnik's indictment I wanted to come and explain what happened to Bosniaks and Croats in certain municipalities. Had the Court invited me to provide explanations for further ethnic groups, I would have done that as well on the basis of the data I've got available. So consequently, I did not prepare to talk about 7.000 witnesses but about tens of thousand victims. I'm talking about victims, not about people who gave testimony about that. So maybe that is what you see as a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again it may be obvious, but excuse me for asking it, but presumably you do have an ethnic breakdown for the 7.000 statements you have taken?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I don't at the moment, but if this Court wants me to do so, I can do it. I had not prepared for that because I always looked at these statements depending on their content and not about -- with regard to the ethnic affiliation of the victims. As to who made the statements, I did not think it was all that important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, when you held those interviews, was it written down somewhere what the ethnicity of your witnesses was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, yes. But considering our method --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out whether this data would be available, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that information in the database as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That data is indeed available and I can make it available to this Court whenever you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear -- Mr. Josse, the data are available. If you think it of sufficient importance, then we'll ask the witness to provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, Mr. Tokaca, are a civil servant. That's what you've told us? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You treat victims in an even-handed manner. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you -- presumably you would not get involved in the politics of your region at all.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: What do you mean? Do you mean if I'm a member of a party or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No I'm not asking you that, let me hastily add. Let me be specific. You remember in 1999 a man called Goran Jelic [sic] stood trial at this court for genocide?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic. Excuse my pronunciation.
